intro/hello: This lecture is about how big models are actually trained: the optimizer, and everything around it.
intro/old: In 2016, the advice fit in one line. Use Adam, and cut the learning rate in steps.
intro/new: A decade later, training a large language model takes five or six moving parts.
intro/adamw: Adam's weight decay turned out to be subtly wrong, and Adam W fixed it.
intro/sched: Fixed steps gave way to a warmup and a long, smooth decay.
intro/clip: Gradients get clipped, so that one bad batch cannot throw the run off a cliff.
intro/bf16: Arithmetic moved to sixteen-bit numbers, which need their own care.
intro/muon: And in late 2024, a new optimizer, Muon, showed that treating a weight matrix as a matrix, not a bag of numbers, trains transformers faster.
intro/plan: Each piece exists because something broke at scale. We take them in order, and spend the most time on Muon.
adamw/recap: First, a recap. Adam keeps two running averages for every parameter.
adamw/m: m is a smoothed gradient. That is momentum.
adamw/v: v is a smoothed squared gradient: how big this parameter's gradients usually are.
adamw/step: Each step divides m by the square root of v, so every parameter takes a step of about the same size, whether its gradients are huge or tiny.
adamw/l2: Now add L two regularization the 2016 way, by putting lambda times w into the gradient.
adamw/sgd: With plain S G D, that is exactly weight decay: every weight shrinks by the same fraction each step.
adamw/problem: With Adam, the decay term also goes through the division by the square root of v.
adamw/big: A weight with large gradients gets its decay divided by a large number, so it nearly vanishes. Tiny gradients amplify it instead.
adamw/demo: Five weights with pure-noise gradients, tiny to large. With L two inside Adam, the tiny-gradient ones collapse to zero, and the large-gradient one barely moves.
adamw/aw: Loshchilov and Hutter, in 2017, moved the decay outside the normalization. That is Adam W.
adamw/same: Now all five shrink along the same curve. It is the default today, typically with weight decay zero point one, on weight matrices only.
schedules/warm: Next, the shape of the learning rate over training. Every large run starts with a warmup.
schedules/why: At step zero, the gradients are large and change fast, and Adam's v rests on only a few samples.
schedules/blow: A full-size step in that state can make the loss spike or diverge.
schedules/ramp: So the learning rate ramps up from almost zero over the first few hundred or thousand steps.
schedules/floor: At the other end, a constant learning rate leaves the weights rattling around the bottom of the loss, at a noise floor set by the step size.
schedules/cos: Cosine decay follows half a cosine wave from the peak down to a small value. GPT three, Chinchilla and Llama all used it.
schedules/catch: Its catch is that you have to know the total number of steps in advance.
schedules/wsd: Warmup, stable, decay, or W S D, holds the peak flat, then cools down fast over the last ten or twenty percent.
schedules/drop: The loss drops sharply during that cooldown, and ends about where cosine does.
schedules/branch: And because the flat phase ignores the total length, you can branch a short decay off any checkpoint, for any budget.
clipping/spikes: Most steps of a big training run look alike. A few do not.
clipping/cause: An unusual batch, or a sharp cliff in the loss, produces a gradient many times larger than usual.
clipping/damage: With S G D, one such step can throw the weights far away. With Adam, it inflates m and v for many steps after.
clipping/norm: The fix starts with the global norm. Square every gradient entry in the whole model, add them all up, and take the square root.
clipping/scale: If that is above a threshold c, usually 1, scale the entire gradient down, so its norm is exactly c.
clipping/dir: Every entry is multiplied by the same number, so the gradient still points the same way. Only its length changes.
clipping/val: Clipping each value on its own is different. It lands on a square instead of a circle, and bends the direction.
clipping/rare: In a healthy run, only a small share of steps get clipped. The ceiling is there for the spikes.
precision/why: Next, the numbers themselves. Sixteen-bit numbers halve the memory, and GPUs multiply them many times faster.
precision/bits: A float has a sign, an exponent that sets its range, and a mantissa that sets its precision.
precision/fp16: F P sixteen has ten mantissa bits, but only five exponent bits. Its largest value is sixty-five thousand, five hundred and four.
precision/bf16: B F sixteen makes the opposite trade: the full eight-bit exponent of F P thirty-two, and only seven mantissa bits.
precision/under: The range problem first. Gradients are often tiny, and in F P sixteen, anything below about six times ten to the minus eight rounds to zero.
precision/hist: Here are typical gradient sizes, on a log scale. In F P sixteen, most of them simply vanish.
precision/scale: Loss scaling fixes this. Multiply the loss by a big power of two before the backward pass, and every gradient moves up into range.
precision/unscale: Divide it back out in F P thirty-two before the update. If anything overflows to infinity, skip the step, and halve the scale.
precision/bf16fix: B F sixteen has the range of F P thirty-two, so it needs no loss scaling at all. That is why it became the default.
precision/gap: Then precision. In B F sixteen, the next number after 1 is about eight thousandths away, so a small update to a weight of 1 rounds away entirely.
precision/master: So the weights live in F P thirty-two as a master copy, with Adam's m and v. Each step casts them to sixteen bits for the forward and backward passes.
matrix/list: So far, parameters have been one long list of numbers. Adam is element-wise: each entry gets its own step size.
matrix/map: But a hidden layer's weight matrix is not a list. It is a linear map, which turns input vectors into output vectors.
matrix/svd: And every matrix can be written as rotate, stretch, rotate. That is the singular value decomposition, U, sigma, V transpose.
matrix/circle: Picture it in two dimensions. The matrix turns the unit circle into an ellipse.
matrix/sv: The stretch factors are the singular values, sigma one and sigma two: how much the matrix stretches each of its special directions.
matrix/outer: The gradient of a linear layer is a sum of outer products: for each example, how its output should change, times its input.
matrix/low: When many examples push the same way, a few singular values dominate. Keller Jordan reported this in transformers: S G D and Adam updates are almost low rank.
matrix/drown: A step shaped like that spends nearly all of its size on a few directions. Rare directions, which may still matter, barely move.
matrix/idea: Muon's idea is simple. Keep the directions, and set every stretch to 1.
muon/name: Muon comes from Keller Jordan and collaborators, in late 2024. The name stands for momentum, orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz.
muon/mom: Start with ordinary momentum: a running sum of recent gradients, kept as a matrix, M.
muon/orth: Then replace M, which is U sigma V transpose, with U V transpose. Same directions, every singular value set to 1.
muon/near: Of all matrices whose singular values are all 1, U V transpose is the closest one to M. This is called orthogonalizing it.
muon/equal: Now the update moves every direction by the same amount, and the rare directions are no longer drowned out.
muon/step: Then take the step, with a small factor for the matrix shape, so that tall matrices get proportionally larger steps.
muon/where: Muon is only for the hidden two-dimensional matrices: the attention projections, and the feed-forward layers.
muon/adamw: Embeddings, the output layer, biases and normalization gains stay on Adam W, so a Muon training loop runs two optimizers.
muon/why: An embedding is a lookup table, not a map on dense vectors. And gains and biases are vectors: there is nothing to orthogonalize.
ns/svd: Computing U V transpose exactly takes an S V D, which is slow on a GPU: it is sequential, and wants thirty-two-bit precision.
ns/mm: Newton-Schulz gets there with nothing but matrix multiplies, which GPUs do at full speed.
ns/key: The key fact: X, times X transpose, times X, keeps every singular direction, and cubes every singular value.
ns/poly: So a mix of X, X cubed and X to the fifth applies one ordinary polynomial to every singular value at once.
ns/norm: First, divide by the norm, so that every singular value is at most 1.
ns/s0: Here is an eight by eight momentum matrix. Normalized, its singular values run from zero point nine five down to one thousandth.
ns/s1: Each step multiplies the small ones by about three point four: the coefficient a, the polynomial's slope at zero.
ns/s3: Step by step, they climb toward 1.
ns/s5: After five steps, seven of eight sit between about zero point seven and one point one, and the smallest has grown four hundred and fifty times.
ns/band: They never land exactly on 1: the coefficients trade exactness for speed, and in practice the band does no harm.
ns/cost: Five steps is fifteen matrix multiplies. With width m and a batch of B tokens, that adds about five m over B: under one percent for real batches.
steepest/choice: Why is this the right update? Taking a step downhill hides a choice: how do you measure the size of a step?
steepest/frob: Measure it by the length of all the entries together, and the best step points straight along the gradient. That is S G D.
steepest/inf: Measure it by the largest single entry, and the best step is the sign of every entry, which is roughly what Adam does.
steepest/spec: Measure it by the spectral norm, the largest singular value, and the best step is U V transpose. That is Muon.
steepest/picture: Here it is in the gradient's own two directions. The disc is every step S G D allows. The square is every step Muon allows.
steepest/corner: The best step in the disc favors the strongest direction. The best step in the square is always the corner: full size in every direction.
steepest/natural: The spectral norm is natural for a linear layer: it bounds how much the layer's output can change, for any input.
steepest/family: This view, from Bernstein and Newhouse in 2024, also links Muon to Shampoo, from 2018: drop Shampoo's memory, and its update is exactly U V transpose.
race/setup: A toy race. Learn a two by two matrix from inputs that vary a lot along one direction, and a thousand times less along another: the rare one.
race/turn: Both directions are turned 45 degrees from the axes, and each optimizer gets its best learning rate from a grid.
race/ellipse: Each ellipse shows what the current W does to the unit circle. The dashed one is the target.
race/sgd: S G D fits the common direction fast, but hardly learns the rare one. Its ellipse stays flat.
race/adam: Adam is no better here. Its per-entry rescaling cannot isolate a direction that is not an axis.
race/muon: Muon equalizes the two directions, and learns both.
race/zero: Turn the rare direction onto an axis, and Adam becomes the best. S G D and Muon do not change at all: neither cares about the basis.
race/caveat: It is a toy that shows the mechanism, not a benchmark. The evidence is in real training runs.
record/speed: Muon came out of the nano G P T speedrun: train a small GPT two sized model to a fixed loss, as fast as possible, on eight H one hundred GPUs.
record/fell: In the second half of 2024, the record fell from about 45 minutes to a few. Muon, introduced that October, was one of the biggest single gains.
record/scale: The open question was scale. In 2025, Moonshot AI found two changes that large runs need.
record/fixes: Add weight decay, as in Adam W. And rescale each matrix's update to the size of AdamW's updates, so its hyperparameters carry over.
record/moonlight: Their scaling experiments then matched Adam W with roughly half the compute, and they trained Moonlight on five point seven trillion tokens.
record/k2: They later trained the trillion-parameter Kimi K two with a Muon variant.
record/rel: Two relatives: Shampoo keeps statistics on both sides of the gradient, and soap runs Adam in the basis they find. Both cost more than Muon.
record/mup: And mu P rescales learning rates with width, so a small model's hyperparameters transfer to a big one. Muon's shape factor has the form it asks for.
outro/recap: So here is the modern recipe, piece by piece.
outro/adamw: Adam W decays every weight by the same fraction, instead of letting Adam's normalization scramble it.
outro/sched: Warmup protects the first steps. Cosine, or warmup-stable-decay, ends at a small learning rate, below the noise floor.
outro/clip: Global norm clipping caps the rare, huge gradient, without turning it.
outro/bf16: B F sixteen computes fast, while F P thirty-two master weights keep the small updates.
outro/muon: And Muon treats each hidden matrix as a map: orthogonalized momentum, computed in five Newton-Schulz steps, for under one percent extra compute.
outro/next: Next, a model too big for one G P U: where all that memory goes, and how the work is split across thousands of them.
